Pontiac, Michigan. Inside the abandoned Pontiac Silverdome.

Before the historic 80,000-seat mega-stadium was imploded, operators from the Naval Special Warfare Development Group (DEVGRU / SEAL Team Six) were given the keys to the entire complex to run unrestricted live-fire counter-terrorism training.

Why an empty NFL stadium?

Because an 80,000-seat concrete dome introduces complex ballistic variables you cannot replicate on a flat shooting range:

Extreme Vertical Angles: Taking steep high-angle sniper shots from the 300-level upper deck down to targets placed on the 50-yard line.

Echoing Acoustics & Concrete Corridors: Navigating disorienting gunshot echoes, cavernous wind drafts, and blind concourse choke points.

Low-Profile Civilian Attire: Notice the operators are wearing blue jeans, flannel shirts, running shoes, and ball caps (including the operator in the foreground rocking a Detroit Lions hat)—matching the blended civilian profile used for domestic counter-terror response.

In the foreground, an operator sits with an Accuracy International precision bolt-action rifle mounted to the railing, while his spotter ranges targets through high-powered glass. Behind him, another team member works barricade transitions with a suppressed weapon platform.

No sterile shoot houses. No computer simulations. Just real-world concrete, steel, and elevation pushed to the absolute limit.

DEVGRU. Always evolving.

Trump is heading to China this week for his third meeting with Xi Jinping in 2026.
Deal or no deal? 

First they met in Beijing in May.
Then in Washington in September.
Now it’s Shenzhen for the APEC summit on November 18-19.

Three face-to-faces in one year between the leaders of the world’s two biggest economies.

Trade. Tariffs. Technology. Rare earths. AI. Influence in the Pacific.
The list of unfinished business is long.

Some people think these meetings are just photo ops.
Others believe this is where the real leverage gets tested — who blinks, who walks away with something concrete, and who just kicks the can further down the road.

After everything that’s happened this year, a third meeting feels less like routine diplomacy and more like a high-stakes checkpoint.

The question isn’t whether they’ll smile for the cameras.
It’s whether anything actually moves.

Deal or no deal?

During high-stakes negotiations in Abu Dhabi mediated by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Washington is urging Moscow to allow European allies a formal seat at the table for upcoming rounds.

While Russia previously pushed to keep talks limited strictly to Washington, Moscow, and Kyiv, American officials insist that lasting security guarantees and regional stability require European leaders in the room.

Can an enduring peace agreement work without Europe at the table? Share your take in the comments below.

CNN is reporting, citing seven U.S. officials, that U.S. intelligence indicates Iran is developing plans to potentially target senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C. — possibly using a "dirty bomb" or a chemical weapon.

Sources stressed the planning appears aimed at giving Tehran options rather than signaling an imminent attack, and officials are still debating whether Iran has the capability or intent to execute it. Still, two sources said the intelligence includes specific targets and locations, prompting contingency meetings over the past week as the Secret Service moved Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other officials into military housing.

White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said the U.S. is "monitoring any and all potential threats, but at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland," while Iran's U.N. Mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations as "false and fabricated."

How seriously should Washington treat this intelligence while Strait of Hormuz talks remain deadlocked?

America’s newest fighter jets just landed in Okinawa…
and they’re replacing more planes than they’re bringing. 

Two brand-new F-15EX Eagle IIs touched down at Kadena Air Base on November 15.
They’re the first of their kind permanently stationed overseas.

The plan is to bring in 36 of these advanced jets to replace the 48 older F-15s that used to call Okinawa home.

Newer technology.
Better sensors.
More weapons capacity.
Stronger electronic warfare systems.

On paper, it’s a clear upgrade.

But the numbers tell a different story too — fewer jets covering the same high-stakes region of the Pacific.

Some see a smarter, more capable force.
Others look at the math and wonder if “better” is enough when you’re still short a dozen aircraft in one of the most contested areas on the planet.

Kadena just got its first look at the future of American airpower in the Pacific.

Big upgrade… or too few jets?

A single line tucked into the U.S. Senate's proposed 2027 budget just revealed $77.1 million for a new nuclear bomb called the B94 — the first new American nuclear bomb designation since 1991.

Under U.S. naming rules, a "B" designation means an air-dropped bomb rather than a missile warhead or a minor upgrade to an existing weapon like the B61-13. Yet the 179-page appropriations document offers zero explanation of what the B94 is designed to do.

Defense analysts say it could be aimed at deeply buried, hardened underground bunkers — a capability gap the U.S. has wrestled with since canceling the Robust Nuclear Earth Penetrator in 2005 — though the Pentagon and NNSA have not confirmed its purpose.

Should the U.S. be developing new nuclear bunker-busters, or sticking to modernizing existing warheads?

While the FAA grounded every flight in America for over 4 hours…
Stephen King had a different explanation. 

On November 13, a nationwide ground stop hit the entire U.S. air system.
Thousands of flights delayed or canceled. Airports frozen. Travelers stuck.

The official reason? A telecommunications outage.

Stephen King wasn’t buying the boring answer.

He posted:
“The aliens have landed. That’s the REAL reason for the ground stop. They don’t want to start a worldwide panic. They are blind but can hear like a motherfucker.”

Only Stephen King could turn a massive aviation meltdown into a horror-story one-liner that millions immediately shared.

Was it just a joke from the master of the creepy?
Or the kind of dark humor that hits a little too close when the whole country suddenly stops flying on a Friday the 13th?

Either way… the man knows how to grab attention.

Do you believe this?

Olympic champion Billy Mills (Oglala Lakota), presented with an Eagle Feather at Lake Andes school.
The only American to ever win Olympic gold in the 10,000 meters.

Billy Mills remains the USA's one and only gold medallist in the men's 10,000m, a feat he achieved at Tokyo 1964.
Run like the wind.

The U.S. Army acknowledged in an urgent contracting notice Friday that American soldiers in the Middle East are "currently at risk" using non-standard personnel shelters made of converted shipping containers.
Now, the Army is moving on an expedited timeline to build 17 reinforced concrete bunkers across five installation sites — one in Israel and two each in Saudi Arabia and Lebanon - within 45 days of a task order.
Each bunker will feature three sections of reinforced concrete, steel entrance doors, concrete Alaska barriers, and sandbagged exterior walls and roofs with at least 18 inches of overhead cover.
Why weren't hardened concrete bunkers already in place before troops were put in shipping container shelters?

VP Vance looked out over the border from a helicopter and said something simple:
“You just needed a new president.” 

No long speech.
No complicated new legislation.
Just a clear statement.

According to Vance, securing the border wasn’t some impossible puzzle that required years of new laws.
It took political will.

He pointed to the lowest border crossings in recent history and the removal of thousands of criminal illegal immigrants as proof that the difference came down to who was in charge.

Some people will hear that and nod.
Others will push back hard and say it’s never that simple.

But the line itself is hard to ignore:
After years of debate, hearings, and failed bills… one side claims the real missing piece was leadership.

Whether you agree or not, it’s a direct challenge to the idea that the border problem was too complex to solve.

Agree?

On October 3, 1993, Chief Warrant Officer Mike Durant was flying Super 64 — an MH-60 Black Hawk with the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment — when an RPG hit the tail rotor over Mogadishu.

The crash killed crewmates Bill Cleveland, Ray Frank, and Tommy Field. Badly injured with a broken back and a compound femur fracture, Durant was defended on the ground by Delta Force snipers Gary Gordon and Randy Shughart, who gave their lives holding the site and were posthumously awarded the Medal of Honor.

Held captive for 11 days, Durant was the only American taken alive that day. He returned to flying, retired in 2001 as a CW4 Master Aviator after 22 years of service including Just Cause and Desert Storm, wrote In the Company of Heroes, built Pinnacle Solutions in Huntsville, and later ran in Alabama's 2022 Republican U.S. Senate primary.

33 years later, his story remains a tribute to the Night Stalkers and Delta operators who never made it home. Night Stalkers Don't Quit.

Leaving the White House for his Asia trip on Monday, President Donald Trump told reporters he "may" bring up the espionage allegations surrounding former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

At the same time, Trump noted that the claims remain unproven — saying, "I don't know that she is a spy. ... Nobody's proven that" — and added he would not mind seeing former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang reinstated.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on November 12 amid reports of his relationship with Alice Huang and U.S. intelligence scrutiny over whether Megaspeed was linked to restricted AI chip transfers. Both Beijing and Megaspeed have denied the allegations, and the Justice Department has not reached a conclusion.

Should Trump raise the Megaspeed and Nvidia investigation directly with Xi Jinping, or keep it separate from trade talks?

Back in June 2012, a Texas father rushed to his 5-year-old daughter's screams on a ranch near Shiner — and caught a 47-year-old acquaintance sexually assaulting her.

The father pulled the man off his child and fatally beat him with his bare hands before calling 911. Lavaca County Sheriff Micah Harmon and District Attorney Heather McMinn confirmed that physical evidence and witness accounts backed up the father's account, and a Lavaca County grand jury declined to bring any charges.

Under Texas law, deadly force is justified when reasonably necessary to stop an ongoing sexual assault or aggravated sexual assault.

Do you agree with the grand jury's decision not to indict?

A #Marine and a #sailor serving with 1st Light Armored Reconnaissance Battalion received the Bronze Star with combat distinguishing device during a ceremony on January 22, 2013.

Sergeant Thaddeus Herber (middle in photo), an infantryman, and Petty Officer 3rd Class Mark Connolly (right in photo), a corpsman, received the Bronze Star from Maj. Gen. Ronald Bailey (left in photo), the commanding general of 1st Marine Division, was awarded the Meritorious Service Medal for their actions in Helmand province, Afghanistan, in 2011.

“THEIR HELICOPTER WAS SHOT DOWN: HE LED THE TEAM RIGHT BACK UP THE MOUNTAIN.”

In the early morning hours of March 4, 2002, atop the freezing, 10,000-foot peak of Takur Ghar in eastern Afghanistan, seven American warriors fought one of the most ferocious, desperate close-quarters battles of Operation Anaconda.

Serving as the team leader of a joint reconnaissance element (Mako 30), Senior Chief Petty Officer Britt K. Slabinski and his Navy SEALs were attempting an insertion when their MH-47E Chinook was ambushed by concealed al-Qaeda fighters firing RPGs and heavy machine guns.

During the evasive maneuvers, Petty Officer First Class Neil Roberts was thrown from the rear ramp into the deep snow. The severely damaged helicopter crash-landed miles away in the valley below.

Knowing Roberts was stranded alone surrounded by an entrenched enemy force, Slabinski didn’t wait for a conventional quick-reaction force. He rallied his five remaining teammates, boarded a second Chinook, and ordered the pilots to fly right back into the teeth of the enemy ambush atop the peak.

What unfolded on that ridge defined the unyielding ethos of the Special Operations community:

Stepping off the helicopter into waist-deep snow and freezing blizzards, the team was instantly met by a barrage of interlocking machine-gun and sniper fire from reinforced bunkers just meters away.

 Slabinski led the charge through the snow, repeatedly exposing himself to direct fire and grenade blasts to engage the bunkers, clear enemy fighting positions, and protect wounded teammates.

Trapped on an open, snow-covered precipice and low on ammunition, Slabinski coordinated precision airstrikes within danger-close range of his own position to prevent the enemy from overrunning their line.

14 Hours on the High Ground: Maneuvering his wounded men to a defensible position under relentless fire, Slabinski directed the medical defense and sustained the perimeter for 14 grueling hours until extraction was secured.

On May 24, 2018, President Donald J. Trump presented Master Chief Britt K. Slabinski with the Medal of Honor at the White House, recognizing his extraordinary valor and refusal to leave a fallen brother behind.

A bond forged in the fires of combat that outlasted the battlefield and saved two lives.

Former DEVGRU (SEAL Team 6) operator Will "Cheese" Chesney seated inside a transport helicopter beside his legendary four-legged teammate, Cairo—the only military working dog on the raid that took down Osama bin Laden.

Pairing up in 2008, Chesney and the Belgian Malinois were virtually inseparable, running hundreds of high-threat direct-action raids across the Global War on Terror. In 2009, Cairo took bullet fire while chasing down enemy insurgents, dragging himself back to Chesney, who fought desperately to keep him alive. Two years later, on the historic night of May 2, 2011, Cairo sat between Chesney’s boots inside a stealth Black Hawk heading into Abbottabad for Operation Neptune Spear—kitted with a Kevlar vest and night vision to secure the perimeter and screen for explosives. In the aftermath of the raid, Cairo was the only operational name released to the public.

The war took a heavy toll on both of them. In 2013, a grenade blast left Chesney with a severe traumatic brain injury and PTSD. As conventional medical treatments failed to break through the crippling migraines and depression, visiting a retired Cairo proved to be his lifeline. Chesney successfully adopted him, allowing the two warriors to nurse each other's scars through Cairo’s final years until cancer claimed the dog in 2015.

Immortalized in Chesney’s memoir No Ordinary Dog, their story stands as the ultimate testament to loyalty between handler and K9.

A man, his dog, and an eternal brotherhood.

Rest in peace, Cairo. The Only Easy Day Was Yesterday. 🇺🇸🔱🐾⚡🦅

Before 300 Blackout and short-barreled MK18s took over modern armories, the gold standard for silent, surgical room-clearing belonged to a German legend: the Heckler & Koch MP5SD.

During the opening years of the Global War on Terror, specialized direct-action elements within U.S. Army Special Forces—specifically Commander’s In-Extremis Force (CIF) and Crisis Response teams—regularly fielded the integrally suppressed 9mm submachine gun for specialized hostage rescue and stealth raids.

Pictured here are 1st Special Forces Group CIF operators (including legendary Green Beret veteran Tu Lam) kitted in classic M81 Woodland, drop-leg holsters, and MP5SDs running clamped dual magazines and early Aimpoint red dots. Thanks to its ported barrel that bleeds supersonic 9mm ammo down to subsonic speeds, the MP5SD delivered surgical accuracy with barely more than the mechanical clatter of its roller-delayed bolt.

Was the MP5SD the greatest close-quarters submachine gun ever engineered, or has modern .300 BLK completely made 9mm subguns obsolete? Drop your thoughts below.

Perched on a jagged cliff edge high above the valley floor.

Private David Paul Twining was an Australian Army infantryman with the 4th Battalion, Royal Australian Regiment (4 RAR), based out of Holsworthy Barracks in Sydney.

In this iconic photograph, Private Twining is seen on a remote mountain observation post (OP):

Camouflaged in Australia's classic DPCU ("Auscam") pattern with field face paint

Gripping an H-250 tactical radio handset to relay intelligence back to command

Armed with the F88 Austeyr bullpup rifle fitted with a dedicated long-range optic

During this era, 4 RAR served at the sharp end of Australian operational deployments, executing peacekeeping, border security, and high-threat reconnaissance missions across the Asia-Pacific region, including East Timor.

This image strips away the noise and shows the raw essence of military service: solitary, patient vigilance on a lonely ridgeline, holding the high ground to protect the mates patrolling down below.

On this day, we pause to honor Private David Paul Twining and all the Australian diggers who stood the watch.

"Lest We Forget."

The Port of New Orleans is suing to seize the tanker that slammed into a docked Mississippi River cruise boat, alleging more than $1 million in terminal damage.

After the Atlantic Asphalt—owned by a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corp.—lost steering and toppled the American Heritage riverboat on Friday, all 197 passengers and crew survived in what officials called the "miracle on the Mississippi." Hours later, port commissioners sued to seize and sell the vessel to cover repairs and salvage costs, and a federal judge approved the seizure warrant.

Should the port be able to seize and auction off the tanker to pay for every dollar of damage? Drop your take below.

#SRSClips #NewOrleans #MississippiRiver

The USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) is reportedly expected to arrive in the Middle East within the next day, putting three U.S. aircraft carriers in the region alongside the USS George Washington and USS George H.W. Bush.

Having departed Singapore on November 9 with Carrier Air Wing 11 aboard, the Roosevelt strike group's arrival comes amid renewed Iranian drone activity toward Bahrain and ongoing naval blockade operations in the Gulf. While the Pentagon has not publicly confirmed whether the Roosevelt will overlap with or relieve the George Washington, concentrating three carrier strike groups signals major U.S. firepower in theater.

Do you think having three carriers in the Middle East will deter Tehran, or is another escalation coming?

Don’t Judge a Book by it’s Cover (The Original Member of Delta Force): Sergeant Major Mike R. Vining enlisted in the U.S. Army in 1968. Following his training, SGM Vining deployed to Vietnam with the 99th Ordnance Detachment (EOD).

In 1978, SGM Vining volunteered for a new unit being formed, the 1st Special Forces Operational Detachment – Delta, where he served until 1985 as the unit’s first EOD specialist. During his assignment, he participated in Operation Eagle Claw in Iran and Operation Urgent Fury in Grenada.

Following an assignment with the 176th Ordnance Detachment (EOD) at Fort Richardson, Alaska, he returned to Delta Force, where he served as Chief EOD Technician, Research and Development Sergeant Major, and Breaching Sergeant Major from 1986 until 1992. During this assignment, he deployed in support of Operation Pocket Planner and Operation Desert Storm.

The B-21 Raider just cleared a major hurdle on its way to combat readiness.

Flying out of Edwards Air Force Base in California, a B-21 test aircraft completed a conventional weapons release test that the U.S. Air Force says transitions the sixth-generation stealth bomber "from flight test to a functional weapons platform." Built on thousands of hours of digital twin modeling, the program remains on track to deliver its first operational bombers to Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027.

Will the B-21 Raider fleet be big enough at 100 aircraft, or does the Air Force need more?

Pete Buttigieg served in Afghanistan, studied at Harvard and Oxford, speaks several languages, and is a husband and dad of twins. Now the former Transportation Secretary says he's leaning toward running for president in 2028—and just announced a new book set for January 2027.

Would you support him in 2028?
Facts….🤣

Maj. John Caldwell, of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for his rapid airpower response to an enemy attack on American and allied forces during his deployment to Nuristan province, Afghanistan, May 2, 2011.

"The DFC is a unique group of individuals; you are about to enjoy elite company like Col. "Bud" Day [retired] who is here today," Col David W. Hicks, 53rd Wing commander and officiator, said to the F-16 pilot before he pinned on the honors.

The F-16 pilot, then rank of captain, responded to an ambush on a special operations team already taking casualties from effective fire. This timely attack allowed the assault team to momentarily regroup.
Hicks was deployed to the area at that time as well and experienced what it

was like to fly three to five hours a day hovering the war zone just in case of emergency.
"At those moments it seemed quiet, like nothing was going on," said the commander as a description of the sortie Air Force pilots perform covering military members on the ground. "But then in 10 to 20 minutes a decision has to be made resulting in life or death."

Caldwell quickly identified mortar flashes from the mountainside, rapidly derived coordinates and directed his wingman to employ a Joint Direct Attack Munition before refueling. According to the award narrative, he remained as the only kinetic asset protecting the assault force.

"I'd like to say I could take the credit, but it took a combined effort of military services to get the team on the ground out of the valley," said Caldwell.

From his F-16 cockpit, the pilot initiated coordination with the Combined Air Operations Center, conveyed the urgent need for medical evacuation and additional kinetic assets. He also contacted the separated assault team's command element, provided real time updates of the dire situation and gained approval to use any ordnance to protect them. Meanwhile, 90 insurgents began a flanking charge on the friendly position.

"Sadly, there were six American and coalition forces I couldn't help that day; they are the true heroes," said Caldwell. "I was at the right place at the right time and I believe anyone in my squadron would do the same thing."

His award citation said the pilot's life was at risk when he employed an immediate, nonstandard, danger close strafe run into the rugged, midnight black valley, breaking the inexorable charge as the enemy continued to fire with rounds impacting mere inches from the trapped allies. Caldwell immediately re-attacked with an expertly placed, danger close JDAM, completely neutralizing the ambush.

All that said, the pilot still would not call himself "hero."

"You don't get to define yourself as a 'hero,' others do," said Hicks. "Specifically, guys on the ground that night are telling the story of the F-16 that saved them and how they wouldn't be standing today, same goes for their families. The fact you did it speaks volumes on who you are as an aviator and what you did for our country."

The DFC narration said, according to the assault force commander, the presence of Caldwell and his immensely accurate awareness of the situation prevented a catastrophic loss of American lives and directly turned the tide of this engagement.

"Caldwell is not only an awesome fighter pilot, he also exemplifies our core value of 'service before self,'" said Lt. Col. Thomas Seymour, commander of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, where Caldwell has served as weapons flight commander since January. "I think this medal is the result of his skill in the air and his willingness to put himself in harm's way in order to accomplish the mission."

In just a short time stationed here, the commander said the pilot won their group's Flight Commander of the Quarter award and fully embraced his new role as an operational test pilot.

Congress authorized The Distinguished Flying Cross, July 2, 1926, as an award for any military member of the U.S. who exhibited heroism or extraordinary achievement while participating in an aerial fight against an enemy of the U.S.

When the drones and missiles hit, he didn’t run.
He ran toward them. 

On March 1, Iranian drones and ballistic missiles slammed into Port Shuaiba in Kuwait.
Six American soldiers never made it home. It remains the deadliest single attack of the conflict.

In the middle of that chaos, Sgt. 1st Class Oscar McGrew took action.
The Army’s own words: “His fearless actions directly saved lives and prevented further casualties during an active enemy attack.”

Last month at Fort Hood, they pinned the Bronze Star with “V” device for valor on his chest.

Most of the details are still locked down out of respect for the families.
But what we do know is enough: when everything was exploding around him, this NCO chose to move toward the danger so others could live.

Some medals get handed out for good paperwork.
This one was earned the hard way.

In most ways, Army Capt. Alex Houston is like any other Army commander. He comes to work every day ready to lead and set the standard for the soldiers who work for him. He diligently performs all of his administrative duties as the 21st Signal Brigade Headquarters and Headquarters Company commander, and he gets down and dirty with the unit during company physical training. He jokes with his staff and even has been known to sing off-key for them.

And he does this all as a wounded warrior. As a platoon leader in Iraq, Houston lost his left hand when his convoy was attacked during a night mission.

The electricity was going on and off while his 1st Cavalry Division unit was on patrol, Houston recalled. “It was so dark -- the kind of dark that you can't even see your hand in front of your face,” he said. As the lights flickered off, the unit's battalion commander came under fire from enemy forces. Although others were in the area, Houston said, he was trained to step up as the ranking officer on the mission, and he headed into the battle to support his commander. He took charge, and while on the radio, he also took a hit.

“There was melted metal all around my hand, and shrapnel went through my arm,” he said, “but I was still on the radio giving information to headquarters.” His duty came before the pain, he said, and his faith in God allowed him to remain calm and accomplish the mission of getting the convoy through the area. “After everyone came over to see how I was, I kept saying, ‘I'm OK.' And I was,” he said. He was rushed to the combat support hospital, and doctors later told him they couldn't save his hand. The division commander presented his Purple Heart while he was still sedated in the combat hospital. “I just said ‘Hooah,'” said Houston, “and they saw the soldier in me.”

Houston spent about a year recovering at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington, D.C. While there, he had access to many programs that helped wounded warriors transition into the civilian job market. But, when the Army asked him if he wanted to stay in, he said he knew his answer was yes. Houston, who started out as an enlisted soldier, already had made a commitment to a career in the Army. “I made a decision a long time ago that I'm going to give 100 percent,” he said. His injury has not been an impediment at all. According to 21st Signal Brigade Commander Col. Theresa Coles, “He's a true testament to the Warrior Ethos."

Mystery drones over a major U.S. air base in England.
Troops ordered to take cover. 

Friday night at RAF Lakenheath — home of the 48th Fighter Wing.
Sirens went off.
Airmen were told to find the nearest shelter.
Suspected unauthorized drones flying over the base.

Security forces responded.
No one was hurt.
No aircraft or infrastructure damaged.
The situation was resolved quickly.

Still… this is one of the largest and most important American fighter bases in Europe.
In a time when threat levels are already elevated.
When planes have been moved around because of potential risks.

Most people will scroll past and say “just another drone scare.”
But when the people who fly F-15s and F-35s are told to get under cover on their own base… it hits different.

Something’s making people nervous out there.

“NO ORDERS. NO BACKUP. I POPPED MY TRUNK, GEARED UP, AND WALKED IN ALONE.” — 22 SAS Hero Christian Craighead on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In one of the most legendary solo counter-terrorism actions in modern military history, former British 22 Special Air Service (SAS) operator Christian Craighead (known across the world as "Obi-Wan Nairobi") broke down the 2019 DusitD2 hotel siege on The Shawn Ryan Show.

In his own words:

“I was off-duty, sitting in traffic in Nairobi having coffee, when the explosions and automatic gunfire echoed across the city.

I didn’t have a mandate. I didn’t have a squad. I had my personal kit and my rifle stashed in the back of my truck. When I drove toward the smoke and saw people running for their lives, covered in blood, screaming that suicide bombers were inside executing hostages floor by floor, there was no deliberation.

You don’t wait for paperwork while innocent people are being slaughtered.

I pulled my body armor on over my civilian clothes, loaded my rifle, and walked past the police cordon into the gunfire by myself. Every instinct built over decades in the Regiment took over: you find the sound of the shooting, you move toward the danger, and you eliminate the threat before they reach another door.”

Throwing on a plate carrier over a purple civilian button-up and blue jeans, Craighead breached the complex alone, clearing rooms, neutralizing multiple Al-Shabaab terrorists, and personally escorting hundreds of terrified civilians to safety.

For his extraordinary individual valor under fire, Craighead was awarded the Conspicuous Gallantry Cross (CGC) by Queen Elizabeth II.

When terror strikes, most run from the gunfire. Men like Christian Craighead pop the trunk and walk straight toward the sound of the guns.

Drop a salute in the comments for 22 SAS operator Christian Craighead.

Barry F. Crawford

HOME OF RECORD: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania

AWARDS BY DATE OF ACTION: Air Force Cross
AWARDED FOR ACTIONS
DURING Global War on Terror
Service: Air Force
Battalion: 21st Special Tactics Squadron

CITATION:
The President of the United States of America, authorized by Title 10, Section 8742, U.S.C., awarded the Air Force Cross to Captain Barry F. Crawford, Jr., for extraordinary heroism in military operations against an armed enemy of the United States as Special Tactics Officer of the 21st Special Tactics Squadron, in action near Laghman Province, Afghanistan, on 4 May 2010. On that date, while attached to Army Special Forces Operational Detachment Alpha and their Afghan partner force, Captain Crawford conducted a helicopter assault into Hendor Village. Upon landing, Captain Crawford received reports that multiple groups of armed enemy were maneuvering into prepared fighting positions in the high ground around the village. As the assault force initiated clearance operations, they began to receive a high volume of accurate machine gun and sniper fire from an enemy force well over 100 fighters. As the assault force was attacked, Captain Crawford took decisive action to save the lives of three wounded Afghan soldiers and evacuate two Afghan soldiers killed in action. Recognizing that the wounded Afghan soldiers would die without evacuation to definitive care, Captain Crawford took decisive action and ran out into the open in an effort to guide the helicopter to the landing zone. Once the pilot had eyes on his position, Captain Crawford remained exposed, despite having one of his radio antennas shot off mere inches form his face, while he vectored in the aircraft. Acting without hesitation, Captain Crawford then bounded across open terrain, engaged enemy positions with his assault rifle and called in AH-64 strafe attacks to defeat the ambush allowing the aid-and-litter teams to move toward the casualties. While the casualties were being moved the team's exposed position once again came under attack from two enemy trucks that had moved into the area and were threatening the medical evacuation landing zone. As one of the aid-and-litter teams was pinned down by enemy fire, and the medical evacuation helicopter took direct hits from small arms fire, it departed with only four casualties leaving one wounded Afghan soldier on the ground. Captain Crawford developed, coordinated, and executed a plan to suppress the enemy, enabling the helicopter to return to the hot landing zone to retrieve the last casualty. While Captain Crawford's element exfiltrated the village, the assault force conducted a two kilometer movement over steep terrain with little to no cover. During this movement the ground force commander and Captain Crawford's element were ambushed and pinned down in the open from multiple enemy fighting positions, some as close as 150 meters away. Without regard for his own life, Captain Crawford moved alone across open terrain in the kill zone to locate and engage enemy positions with his assault riffle while directing AH-64 30-mm. strafe attacks. Continuing to move the team further over 1.5 kilometers of steep terrain with minimal cover, Captain Crawford again engaged the enemy with his assault rifle while integrating AH-64s and F-15E's in a coordinated air-to-ground attack plan that included strafing runs along with 500 and 2,0000-pound bomb and Hellfire missile strikes. Throughout the course of the ten hour firefight, Captain Crawford braved effective enemy fire and consciously placed himself at grave risk on four occasions while controlling over 33 aircraft and more than 40 air strikes on a well-trained and well-prepared enemy force. His selfless actions and expert airpower employment neutralized a numerically superior enemy force and enabled friendly elements to exfiltrate the area without massive casualties. Through his extraordinary heroism, superb airmanship, and aggressiveness in the face of the enemy, Captain Crawford has reflected great credit upon himself and the United States Air Force.

The man who played Jesus just said there’s a fatwa on his head.

Jim Caviezel told Benny Johnson flat out: “I have a fatwa on me.”

He claims some Muslims want him dead because of a 2009 film he did called The Stoning of Soraya M. — the true story of an Iranian woman falsely accused of adultery and publicly stoned to death.
According to Caviezel, that movie “exposed them,” and under their belief system they now have the right to “cut my heart out.”

No independent confirmation of an actual fatwa has been reported. It’s his claim.
Still, the actor who once carried the cross on screen is now saying the price of telling certain stories might be his own life… and warning that most Americans don’t understand what Sharia really means yet.

Some people will call it fear-mongering.
Others will say he’s the only one still willing to say it out loud.

“HE SAW THE WIRE AND BOMB UNDER THE CLOAK: HE TACKLED HIM WITH HIS BARE HANDS.”

On August 8, 2012, in the crowded streets of Asadabad, Kunar Province, Afghanistan, a joint patrol of American commanders and provincial leaders was walking toward the provincial governor’s compound when an unthinkable threat emerged.

Serving as the personal security detachment commander for the 4th Infantry Division's 4th Brigade Combat Team, Captain Florent “Flo” Groberg was scanning the perimeter when he noticed an individual acting suspiciously on the left side of the street, walking backward toward the patrol formation.

As the man pivoted, Groberg spotted a suicide bomb vest concealed under the man’s cloak, complete with protruding trigger wires.

With less than two seconds to react, Captain Groberg made an instantaneous decision that saved dozens of lives:

Charging the Threat: Groberg yelled a warning, abandoned cover, and charged straight at the bomber, physically shoving him backward away from the command group.

Tackling Him to the Ground: Teaming up with Sergeant Andrew Mahoney, Groberg drove the bomber into the dirt, pinning the vest against the ground with his bare hands to absorb the blast.

Disrupting the Attack: The vest detonated against the earth. The downward blast blew Groberg 20 feet into a culvert, severing 50% of his calf muscle, shattering his fibula, and causing severe burns, but preventing the primary fragmentation wave from tearing through the command group.

Triggering the Second Bomber: The shockwave caused a second concealed suicide bomber nearby to detonate prematurely into an exterior wall before he could reach the patrol.

Four American heroes were killed in the ambush—Command Sgt. Maj. Kevin J. Griffin, Maj. Thomas E. Kennedy, Air Force Maj. Walter D. Gray, and foreign service officer Ragaei Abdelfattah—but dozens more survived because Captain Groberg physically threw his body onto the threat.

On November 12, 2015, President Barack Obama presented Captain Florent Groberg with the Medal of Honor at the White House.

U.S. Army Lieutenant Colonel Kathryn Van Auken and Major Lauralee Flannery were awarded the Bronze Star with "V" for valor for their sustained courage and heroic performance of duties during Operation Iraqi Freedom.

Van Auken and Flannery had been serving together in Iraq in support of a Kuwait Exploitation Team's objective to secure, safeguard, and assist a Kuwait forensic team in the recovery of the remains of Kuwaiti Prisoners of War and Missing from the end of the 1991 Gulf War.

Van Auken and Flannery were traveling together in the lead vehicle on February 14, 2007. They had been tasked with escorting the Kuwait Forensic Team's convoy of 12 vehicles.

It was approximately 7:30 a.m. when the middle four vehicles of the convoy were hit with the largest planned improvised explosive device (IED) attack that had been recorded up until that time.

Ten daisy-chained 155mm mortar rounds had been buried under the raised causeway they were traveling on south of Razzazah Lake in the vicinity of Karbala, Iraq.

When these IEDs exploded, three vehicles were destroyed, and passengers -- disoriented and bleeding -- began exiting their vehicles.

We both exited our vehicle," Van Auken said. "[MAJ Flannery] headed east and I headed west trying to gather up everyone and secure both ends of the roadway against secondary attacks."

As team leader, Van Auken deployed rapidly, undertaking a multiplicity of actions, quickly radioing instructions to move all vehicles through the smoke and debris and to follow her vehicle into safety away from the IED site to avoid secondary devices.

In this highly fluid situation, vehicles became disabled. Van Auken and Flannery quickly ordered the destroyed vehicles to be pushed out of the kill zone by follow on vehicles in the convoy in order to assemble the team and get everyone to a safe and secure distance.

Van Auken then maneuvered the front column of Polish security elements and Korean Engineer vehicles into security postures along the west side of the raised causeway with great speed and determination, gaining the advantage against any follow-on IED or possible ambush.

Both soldiers reacted fearlessly and without hesitation, running alone down the west end of the roadway to halt any oncoming traffic, orienting Iraqi vehicles to block the road, dismissing large crowds gathering, and re-positioning Polish security forces to assist.

The team provided medical assistance to their Kuwaiti team members who had been badly cut with glass and debris and who were vomiting and shaking on the side of the road from the shocking experience.

Their actions provided an example of urgency and purpose to fellow coalition forces, and their courage under fire unquestionably saved the lives of coalition forces, particularly the civilians in their charge.

" We are battle buddies to the end," Van Auken said.

“HE HAD A FRACTION OF A SECOND TO SAVE HIS MEN. HE CHOSE TO SACRIFICE HIMSELF.” — The Courage of Marine Corporal Jason Dunham.

On April 14, 2004, near the Syrian border in Husaybah, Iraq, 22-year-old Marine Corporal Jason Dunham was leading a rifle squad with 3rd Battalion, 7th Marines (3/7), moving to relieve a battalion commander’s convoy that had been ambushed.

After intercepting a line of suspicious vehicles attempting to flee the area, Dunham moved in on foot to conduct a search:

 As Dunham approached, an insurgent leaped from one of the vehicles and attacked him. Dunham immediately engaged the fighter in violent hand-to-hand combat to subdue him.

During the wrestling match on the dirt road, the insurgent pulled the pin on a hand grenade and dropped it between them.

Spotting two of his Marines—Lance Corporal William Hampton and PFC Kelly Miller—rushing in to assist him, Dunham shouted a warning: “No, no, watch out!” Without hesitation, he unstrapped his Kevlar helmet, slammed it over the grenade, and threw his entire body on top, pressing down with both hands to smother the blast.

The grenade exploded, shredding the helmet and mortally wounding Dunham. But his body and helmet absorbed the overwhelming force of the blast, saving both of his fellow Marines from fatal shrapnel.

Corporal Dunham was evacuated and succumbed to his wounds eight days later on April 22, 2004, at Bethesda Naval Hospital with his parents at his bedside.

On January 11, 2007, President George W. Bush presented the Medal of Honor posthumously to his family, making Jason Dunham the first Marine in the Iraq War to receive the nation’s highest military decoration. His legacy lives on across the fleet aboard the guided-missile destroyer USS Jason Dunham (DDG-109).

In an era where so few bear the burden of service, what does Corporal Jason Dunham’s split-second decision to smother a live grenade tell us about the heart of an American Marine?

“23 POUNDS OF STEEL. HUNDREDS OF ROUNDS OF 7.62. WELCOME TO THE JUNGLE.” — The Brutal Reality of Humping “The Pig” in Vietnam.

In the dense, suffocating heat of the Vietnamese jungle, infantrymen gave the M60 machine gun a nickname that stuck for generations: “The Pig.”

It earned the name honestly—because of its bulky, cumbersome weight, ferocious appetite for belted ammunition, and bone-jarring recoil when ripping through the brush:

• The Physical Punishment: At 23.15 pounds unloaded, the M60 was already a beast to carry. Factor in a spare barrel, an asbestos heat mitt, cleaning kit, and 500 to 1,000 rounds of linked 7.62×51mm NATO ammunition draped in crisscrossed bandoliers across the gunner and assistant gunner's chests, and a gun team was humping 70+ pounds through chest-high, razor-sharp elephant grass and knee-deep mud in 100-degree humidity.

• The Squad’s Lifeline: Firing at a sustained 550 to 650 rounds per minute with an effective range of over 1,100 meters, the M60 was the squad's primary base of fire. When an infantry patrol walked into an L-shaped ambush in the triple canopy, the distinctive heavy thumping roar of "The Pig" chewing through tree trunks was the only thing that bought troops time to maneuver.

• The Quirks: Early models lacked a carrying handle on the barrel, forcing gunners to use a bulky asbestos mitt to swap out glowing-red barrels mid-firefight. It was prone to jamming in red clay dust and mud, but when properly cleaned and fed, it delivered unmatched stopping power.

To the veterans who carried or fought alongside "The Pig" in Vietnam, the Gulf, or beyond: did you love it for its devastating firepower, or curse it every time you had to hump it up a ridgeline?

#Marines, Staff Sgt. Juan Rodrigues-Chavez (left) and Capt. Adeomola Fabayo received the Navy Cross at the National Museum of the Marine Corps on June 10, 2011, for their heroic actions in Afghanistan's Kunar Province in September 2009.

June 12, 2011 -- For two Marines attached to Marine Embedded Training Team 2-8, Regional Corps Advisory Command 3-7, in Kunar Province, Afghanistan, the morning of Sept. 8, 2009 started simple enough.

Then the world exploded around them.

Their actions during the ensuing fight earned them the nation’s second-highest award for valor. Secretary of the Navy Ray Mabus presented Capt. Ademola D. Fabayo and Staff Sgt. Juan J. Rodriguez-Chavez with the Navy Cross during a ceremony at the National Museum of the Marine Corps on June 10.

On that fateful day, then 1st Lt. Fabayo was leading a dismounted patrol of Americans and two platoons of Afghan National Security Forces into Ganjgal Village for a pre-dawn meeting with village elders. A short distance away, Rodriguez-Chavez was part of the team’s security element, ready to help his teammates if necessary.

The team was attacked by more than 50 enemy fighters, who rained down machine gun fire and rocket-propelled grenades from fortified positions. Four members of the team were cut off and exposed to the murderous fire.

With no regard for his own life, Fabayo pushed forward on foot into the kill zone in an attempt to regain contact, effectively engaging the enemy at close range with his M4 rifle. When a U.S. Army advisor was severely wounded, Fabayo moved from a covered position under heavy fire to assist in his recovery, helping carry him across several hundred meters of fire-swept ground.

He then gotten into an unarmored truck with another advisor and pushed back into the kill zone, ignoring the rounds striking the truck, as they attempted to rescue the fallen members of their team.

While Fabayo was attacking, Rodriguez-Chavez wasted no time getting into the fight as well. With members of his team in immediate danger, he drove a gun truck, with one other Marine as his gunner, forward into the kill zone of the ambush with only the machine gun fire of his gunner to suppress the enemy. He repeatedly ignored the heavy enemy fire and drove the vehicle into the kill zone three times to cover the withdrawal of the force and evacuate two dozen members of the Afghan National Security Forces.

The two Marines, along with two other members of their team, then consolidated their force into an armored Humvee, Rodriguez-Chavez at the wheel and Fabayo in the gunners turret, manning the machine gun. They made yet another extremely hazardous trip into the deepest point of the kill zone, where Rodriguez-Chavez positioned his vehicle to shield his teammates from the intense enemy fire as they dismounted to recover the fallen warriors.

During the ceremony, Mabus said that the Marines repeatedly exposed themselves to enemy fire and demonstrated the kind of valor that should be taught to every Marine in boot camp.

Maj. John Caldwell, of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for his rapid airpower response to an enemy attack on American and allied forces during his deployment to Nuristan province, Afghanistan, May 2, 2011.

"The DFC is a unique group of individuals; you are about to enjoy elite company like Col. "Bud" Day [retired] who is here today," Col David W. Hicks, 53rd Wing commander and officiator, said to the F-16 pilot before he pinned on the honors.

The F-16 pilot, then rank of captain, responded to an ambush on a special operations team already taking casualties from effective fire. This timely attack allowed the assault team to momentarily regroup.
Hicks was deployed to the area at that time as well and experienced what it

was like to fly three to five hours a day hovering the war zone just in case of emergency.
"At those moments it seemed quiet, like nothing was going on," said the commander as a description of the sortie Air Force pilots perform covering military members on the ground. "But then in 10 to 20 minutes a decision has to be made resulting in life or death."

Caldwell quickly identified mortar flashes from the mountainside, rapidly derived coordinates and directed his wingman to employ a Joint Direct Attack Munition before refueling. According to the award narrative, he remained as the only kinetic asset protecting the assault force.

"I'd like to say I could take the credit, but it took a combined effort of military services to get the team on the ground out of the valley," said Caldwell.

From his F-16 cockpit, the pilot initiated coordination with the Combined Air Operations Center, conveyed the urgent need for medical evacuation and additional kinetic assets. He also contacted the separated assault team's command element, provided real time updates of the dire situation and gained approval to use any ordnance to protect them. Meanwhile, 90 insurgents began a flanking charge on the friendly position.

"Sadly, there were six American and coalition forces I couldn't help that day; they are the true heroes," said Caldwell. "I was at the right place at the right time and I believe anyone in my squadron would do the same thing."

His award citation said the pilot's life was at risk when he employed an immediate, nonstandard, danger close strafe run into the rugged, midnight black valley, breaking the inexorable charge as the enemy continued to fire with rounds impacting mere inches from the trapped allies. Caldwell immediately re-attacked with an expertly placed, danger close JDAM, completely neutralizing the ambush.

All that said, the pilot still would not call himself "hero."

"You don't get to define yourself as a 'hero,' others do," said Hicks. "Specifically, guys on the ground that night are telling the story of the F-16 that saved them and how they wouldn't be standing today, same goes for their families. The fact you did it speaks volumes on who you are as an aviator and what you did for our country."

The DFC narration said, according to the assault force commander, the presence of Caldwell and his immensely accurate awareness of the situation prevented a catastrophic loss of American lives and directly turned the tide of this engagement.

"Caldwell is not only an awesome fighter pilot, he also exemplifies our core value of 'service before self,'" said Lt. Col. Thomas Seymour, commander of the 85th Test and Evaluation Squadron, where Caldwell has served as weapons flight commander since January. "I think this medal is the result of his skill in the air and his willingness to put himself in harm's way in order to accomplish the mission."

In just a short time stationed here, the commander said the pilot won their group's Flight Commander of the Quarter award and fully embraced his new role as an operational test pilot.

Congress authorized The Distinguished Flying Cross, July 2, 1926, as an award for any military member of the U.S. who exhibited heroism or extraordinary achievement while participating in an aerial fight against an enemy of the U.S.

A FASCINATING MILITARY RANK SHOWDOWN

A compelling dynamic is unfolding in Washington as retired U.S. Navy Rear Admiral Nancy Lacore mounts a bid for Congress that could place her in a direct oversight role over Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

If elected to the House of Representatives, Admiral Lacore would become the highest-ranking female military officer ever to serve in the United States Congress.

In terms of military service, the rank difference is substantial. Hegseth served honorably as an Army National Guard Major (O-4), deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan. Lacore reached the rank of Two-Star Rear Admiral (O-8), serving decades as a naval aviator and flag officer.

While the Secretary of Defense holds ultimate civilian authority over the armed forces, having a retired Two-Star admiral on Capitol Hill creates a rare dynamic in congressional oversight of the Pentagon.

Does a higher military rank make someone a more qualified voice on defense policy, or does field-grade combat experience better represent the frontline warfighter?
